angle: The 3 buckets of signals: out-of-the-box, custom, and first-party
post_first_line: 3 buckets of signals. That's the whole model.
linkedin_post:
3 buckets of signals. That's the whole model.

Cole Courson breaks every signal into three categories, and the third one is where it gets interesting.

Bucket one is out-of-the-box signals. Website intent tracking, persona-level tracking, champion tracking, new hires, job changes. Providers like Unify, Clay, and 6sense offer these. Flip the switch and they work.

Cole says they're interesting at layer 1, but they get more valuable when compounded with other signals.

Bucket two is custom signals. Technographics. Job scraping, like hiring for specific roles. Social listening on Reddit, GitHub, and Glassdoor to find pain.

Cole calls these really important to dive into.

There could be more than three buckets. Cole prefers to simplify into three.

Which bucket is your team leaning on most?

Slide 3: Website intent, persona tracking, champion tracking, new hires, job changes

Slide 8: There could be more buckets. Simple beats complete.

lesson.title: Simplify your signals into buckets
takeaways: Out-of-the-box signals like intent, champion tracking, and job changes are quick to turn on but are just layer 1.
Custom signals like technographics, job scraping, and social listening on Reddit, GitHub, and Glassdoor surface pain.
Signals get more interesting when compounded rather than used alone.
lesson.exercise: List every signal your team currently tracks. Sort each into out-of-the-box or custom, then pick one signal from each bucket to combine.

angle: Two things Google flags in high-volume cold email, and how to avoid them
post_first_line: 400k emails a month changes how Google sees you.
linkedin_post:
400k emails a month changes how Google sees you.

That's 9 words, so it needs trimming to 8 or fewer. 

Revised:

High volume changes how Google sees you.

Cole Courson shared two things Google flags in high-volume cold email, and one of them is easy to miss.

The first is sameness. When every email looks identical to the next, that's a signal. Cole's fix for broader campaigns in the 200k to 400k a month range is to build in variability with dynamic snippets: first name, last name, company name, sender name, and spintax.

Small differences from one email to the next make it much easier to land at scale.

The second is a mismatch between subject line and body. If the subject line says one thing and the message is about something else, Google can flag it as spam.

So the subject has to match what the email actually delivers.

Neither fix is complicated. Both are easy to skip when you're pushing volume.

What's your go-to snippet for adding variability?

Slide 2: Google flags emails that look identical to each other.
Slide 3: Fix it with variability from one email to the next.
Slide 4: Use first name, last name, company, and sender name snippets.
Slide 5: Add spintax to vary the copy itself.
Slide 6: Google also flags subject lines that don't match the body.
Slide 7: If the subject promises one thing, the email must deliver it.
Slide 8: Small details decide whether you land at scale.

lesson.title: Two Spam Flags in High-Volume Cold Email
takeaways: Google flags a lack of variability between one email and the next, so build it in with dynamic snippets.
Snippets like first name, last name, company name, sender name, and spintax make large campaigns land better.
A subject line that disconnects from the body of the message can also be flagged as spam.
lesson.exercise: Open your highest-volume campaign and add at least three variable elements, such as first name, company name, and a spintax phrase. Then reread each subject line against its body and rewrite any that don't match.

angle: Why one big send day can get your mailboxes cancelled and cost you a month of warmup
post_first_line: One big send day can cost a month.
linkedin_post:
One big send day can cost a month.

Cole Courson has seen how one decision like that plays out.

Say a team sends 50 emails a day, every day. Then someone decides to promote a webinar to 100,000 people. Google flags the break in the pattern.

The result: mailboxes get cancelled and domains get shut down.

Warming up domains typically takes 2 to 3 weeks. So the damage goes beyond messages landing in spam or disappearing into the ether. The team then spends a month warming everything back up.

Cole has been through that process and calls it really, really painful.

Google watches for consistency in daily send volume. Treat that consistency as an asset you protect.

To push toward larger volumes, scale up gradually instead of in one jump.

Have you ever had to rebuild a burned domain?

lesson.title: Consistent send volume protects your mailboxes
takeaways: Google flags sudden changes in daily send volume, not just high volume.
A single spike can get mailboxes cancelled and domains shut down.
Warming domains typically takes 2 to 3 weeks, so recovery costs about a month.
lesson.exercise: Write down your current daily send volume per mailbox, then plan a gradual ramp toward your target volume instead of one large jump.

angle: 'Saw you on our website' is lazy: give prospects a real reason to talk to you
post_first_line: "Saw you on our website" is lazy.
linkedin_post:
"Saw you on our website" is lazy.

Bobby Foose has a blunt take on why most outreach gets ignored.

Bobby's starting point: put yourself in the other person's shoes. Why would they want to talk to you? A very valid answer is that they don't.

So the job is to give them a reason that goes beyond "saw you on our website." That line shows zero homework.

Bobby's example is much simpler and more human: "Hey, you're from the same hometown as Bobby. Bobby is out in San Francisco now, working at a startup called Unify."

A real connection comes first. The rest can follow.

The bar for a good opener isn't high. It takes a few minutes of actual effort to show the person on the other end the work was done.

What's the best cold opener you've ever received?

lesson.title: Give prospects a real reason to talk to you
takeaways: Assume the prospect has no inherent reason to talk to you.
"Saw you on our website" signals zero homework.
A genuine personal connection earns attention before the pitch.
lesson.exercise: Pick five prospects you plan to contact this week. For each one, find one real personal or professional connection, like a hometown, shared background, or mutual interest, and rewrite your opener around it.

angle: Stop obsessing over Gmail vs Outlook: org size and a single channel are the bigger deliverability problem
post_first_line: Gmail vs Outlook is the wrong deliverability fight.
linkedin_post:
Gmail vs Outlook is the wrong deliverability fight.

Cole Courson sees a bigger variable most teams skip past.

Org size. Emailing into large organizations is just tougher. They run spam checkers and blockers, and sometimes pay for platforms that stop outside emails from getting through.

So Cole's advice: keep the best practices as your first focus, then worry more about those nuances than which inbox provider sits on the other end.

The other piece is channel. Email alone is a narrow bet.

Use signals and intent to send a strong email. Then refer to that email in a cold call, so the rep gets a real opening instead of a cold start.

Cole called it out directly: even in an email course, the recommendation is to use all three channels.

When email stalls at a big account, which channel do you add first?

Slide 2: Org size is the bigger variable most teams overlook.
Slide 3: Large companies run spam checkers and blockers on inbound email.

Slide 5: Best practices still come first. Get those right.
Slide 6: Then use signals and intent to send a good email.
Slide 7: Reference that email in a cold call to open the conversation.
Slide 8: Email-only is a narrow bet. Use all three channels.

lesson.title: Deliverability Is Bigger Than Your Inbox Provider
takeaways: Emailing into large organizations is tougher because of spam checkers, blockers, and paid filtering platforms.
Best practices remain the first place to focus, before chasing nuances.
Multichannel lets a signal-driven email set up a cold call that gets a real opportunity.
lesson.exercise: Pick five large accounts where email is getting no replies. For each, write one email based on a signal, then draft a cold call opener that references that email.

angle: 300-400K emails a month run by one orchestrator, and why a case study like that belongs in your email framework
post_first_line: 300 to 400K emails a month. One orchestrator.
linkedin_post:
300 to 400K emails a month. One orchestrator.

Cole Courson says that setup is exactly the kind of story that belongs in your email framework.

For one Guru point of contact, Cole runs roughly 300 to 400K emails a month with a single orchestrator. That saves time and energy, and still drives marketing results.

Cole's point: a result like that becomes a clean case study. A typical email framework includes the question of what story you've already helped a company like that tell.

But the story is not where you start. Before writing email one for founder-led sales, Cole says you need to know where you want to begin.

That means getting clear on the personas, the splits, the pains, and the stories.

The copy comes after that groundwork.

What's your strongest case study for outbound?

takeaways: A clean, high-volume result makes a strong case study for your email framework.

Founder-led sales emails start with clarity on personas, splits, pains, and stories, not copy.
lesson.exercise: Write down your top customer result in one sentence, then map it to a persona and a pain. Place it in your email framework as the story step before drafting email one.
